stem: Which of the following sudden combinations should make a bystander suspect a stroke?

options.label: A
options.text: Bilateral calf soreness after a long walk
options.misconception: Expected exertional discomfort is being confused with an abrupt focal neurologic deficit.
options.explanation: The CDC warning pattern is sudden one-sided weakness or numbness and trouble speaking, not bilateral soreness after exertion.

options.label: B
options.text: One-sided face or arm weakness with trouble speaking
options.misconception: None; sudden unilateral weakness and speech difficulty are stroke warning signs.
options.explanation: Sudden weakness or numbness affecting one side of the face, arm, or leg together with trouble speaking should raise immediate concern for stroke.

options.label: C
options.text: Gradual wrist stiffness after repetitive computer work
options.misconception: A gradual local musculoskeletal complaint is being treated as an acute focal neurologic event.
options.explanation: Stroke warning signs begin suddenly and include one-sided weakness or numbness and speech difficulty, unlike gradual wrist stiffness.

options.label: D
options.text: Itchy eye redness with seasonal nasal congestion
options.misconception: An allergic symptom cluster is being mistaken for focal neurologic dysfunction.
options.explanation: Eye itch and nasal congestion do not match the cited sudden unilateral weakness and speech warning pattern.

options.label: E
options.text: Brief finger tingling after leaning on an elbow
options.misconception: Position-related tingling in one small nerve territory is being overgeneralized to a stroke pattern.
options.explanation: The CDC pattern involves sudden face, arm, or leg weakness or numbness, especially on one side, often with trouble speaking.

context: Learning objective: recognize a stroke warning pattern. Sudden one-sided face, arm, or leg weakness or numbness plus new difficulty speaking is an emergency signal, not something to watch casually.
